items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: Where necessary, the controller shall carry out a review to assess if processing is performed in accordance with the data protection impact assessment
items.why: The binding rule: assess before high-risk processing (35(1)), minimum contents (35(7)), review when the risk changes (35(11)). The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 did not alter the duty; the only change since 2020 is 'Commission' in 35(4) and (5), substituted 30 September 2026 by S.I. 2026/386. No outstanding changes shown on the day checked.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 83: General conditions for imposing administrative fines
items.quote: the obligations of the controller and the processor pursuant to Articles 8, 11, 25 to 39 and 42 and 43
items.why: Places Article 35 in the lower of the two penalty tiers. The amount is not repeated in the brief because another brief already uses it.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: What is a DPIA?
items.quote: a DPIA is not simply a rubber stamp or a technicality as part of a sign-off process
items.why: States that outcomes must be integrated back into the project plan and that the assessment is a 'living' process to be reviewed when anything changes. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act; no date on the page, so the year is the year read.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: When do we need to do a DPIA?
items.locator: Sections 'What other factors might indicate likely high risk?' and 'What does the ICO consider likely to result in high risk?'
items.quote: In most cases, a combination of two of these factors indicates the need for a DPIA.
items.why: The screening test. Lists the regulator's ten extra triggers; innovative technology (including AI) requires an assessment when combined with one other criterion, and automated decisions on access to a service require one outright. Says a decision not to assess should be documented. 'Under review' banner; undated page.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: How do we do a DPIA?
items.locator: Sections 'Step 7: How do we conclude our DPIA?' and 'What happens next?'
items.quote: You should identify any action points and who is responsible for implementing them.
items.why: The regulator's seven steps and what happens after sign-off: outcomes go into the project plan, actions have owners, the assessment is kept under review. It asks for an owner per action; it does not ask for dates or closure evidence. 'Under review' banner; undated page.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.locator: Section 'What do we need to consider when undertaking data protection impact assessments for AI?'
items.quote: the use of AI will involve a type of processing likely to result in a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms
items.why: Source of the statement that the great majority of AI uses trigger the duty, and that a decision that a use is not high risk must still be documented. Asks for evidence of less risky alternatives considered, and for review as populations and behaviour shift. 'Under review' banner; latest update shown is 15 March 2023.

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.quote: AI providers had completed DPIAs retrospectively or just prior to the audit
items.why: What the regulator found when it read real assessments: some done after the fact, some undated, many lacking necessity and alternatives, few recording what changed after consultation, most not regularly reviewed once the tool was live (p. 36). Findings are qualitative; no counts are given for this section.

items.title: Decision of the Information Commissioner: Snap Inc. and Snap Group Limited
items.quote: a cursory and higher-level risk assessment, in tabular format
items.why: Source of the quotation and the figure. A preliminary enforcement notice (6 October 2023) alleged breach of Articles 35 and 36; the firm produced a fifth assessment on 22 November 2023, which was accepted, so no enforcement notice was issued and no infringement was finally found. Shows the regulator reading an assessment line by line against Article 35(7). Redacted public version.

items.title: Guidelines on Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and determining whether processing is "likely to result in a high risk" for the purposes of Regulation 2016/679 (WP 248 rev.01)
items.publisher: Article 29 Data Protection Working Party (European Commission)
items.locator: Section III.D(a), p. 14; nine criteria at pp. 9-11; Annex 2 (criteria for an acceptable DPIA)
items.quote: Carrying out a DPIA is a continual process, not a one-time exercise.
items.why: The European guidelines that the UK regulator's trigger list is built on, and whose Annex 2 it recommends as a quality checklist. Not binding in the UK since exit; the UK regulator says such guidelines may still be helpful.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 27: Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment
items.why: International comparator: a second assessment for certain deployers of high-risk systems (public bodies, private providers of public services, and deployers of the systems in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III), which may draw on the data protection assessment. This is the Commission's copy, not the Official Journal; it carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and may not be fully updated. Paragraphs 4 and 5 are marked 'AMENDED'. No application date is stated here.

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.locator: Ground 3, paras 145 to 154; quote at para 153; order, para 1
items.quote: the DPIA failed properly to assess the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
items.why: The leading UK judgment on what makes an impact assessment inadequate. The police force had written one for live facial recognition, and the lower court accepted it; the Court of Appeal held it deficient. The assessment proceeded on the footing that privacy rights were not infringed, when the court had found the rules left too much discretion over who went on watchlists and where cameras were used; so it had not properly assessed the risks or the measures to address them. An assessment that exists can still fail. Limits: decided under section 64 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (law enforcement processing), not UK GDPR Article 35, though the required contents are closely similar; a 2020 judgment on one force's trials.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 64: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: the controller must, prior to the processing, carry out a data protection impact assessment
items.why: The duty the court applied in Bridges: for law enforcement processing likely to result in high risk, an assessment before processing that covers the operations, the risks to people, the measures to address them and the safeguards. Shows the 'before, not after' rule is statute in both UK regimes. Limits: Part 3 only (competent authorities processing for law enforcement purposes). In force 25 May 2018; no amendment notes on the section.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 36: Prior consultation
items.quote: would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk
items.why: The consequence of an honest assessment: if it shows a high risk that the controller's measures do not reduce, the regulator must be consulted before processing starts, and may give written advice within eight weeks, extendable by six. This is what 'acted on' means at the top of the scale. Limits: the text now reads 'the Commission' following the change of regulator; how often prior consultation is used in practice was not found.

items.title: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services. 2. Data protection impact assessments
items.locator: Standard 2, opening statement and 'What do you mean by a DPIA?'; 'When do we need to do a DPIA?'
items.quote: You should begin a DPIA early in the design of your service, before you start your processing.
items.why: A statutory code of practice that makes the impact assessment its second standard for any online service children are likely to use; a consumer AI product that children are likely to use would be in scope. It requires a new assessment before significant changes to an existing service and says outside events, such as a new public concern, may prompt a review. Limits: applies to online services likely to be accessed by children; the page prints no date (page metadata 17 December 2025, used for the year); the date the code was issued is not shown on this page.

items.title: Reprimand: Chelmer Valley High School
items.quote: no DPIA had been completed for the introduction of facial recognition technology prior to the processing commencing in March 2023
items.why: A UK enforcement outcome where the formal finding is a breach of Article 35(1) itself, which the first research pass did not find. A school brought in facial recognition for about 1,200 pupils in March 2023 and completed its assessment in November 2023; the regulator said an assessment done first would have exposed the consent failures that followed. Limits: a reprimand to a school, with no fine; biometric recognition, not a decision-making system; filed under 'regulator guidance' because the type list has no value for enforcement action. The 22 July 2024 date is from the regulator's enforcement page; the PDF file name carries 2 July.

items.title: Carrying out a data protection impact assessment if necessary (AI how-to sheets)
items.publisher: Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL)
items.locator: Introduction and section 'The realisation of a DPIA for the development of AI systems'
items.quote: should be changed iteratively as the characteristics of the processing and risk assessment evolve
items.why: AI-specific guidance on impact assessments from a major European regulator. It says building a training dataset can itself create high risk, applies the two-criteria screening rule to AI development, and deals with the case where the developer cannot foresee the deployed use: the developer assesses development and the deploying organisation completes the picture. Supports the 'currency' level of the criterion. Limits: French regulator, EU GDPR; a courtesy translation, with the French text prevailing. Not binding in the UK.

items.title: Guide to undertaking privacy impact assessments
items.publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
items.locator: Section 'When to do a PIA'; footnote 3 on the Australian Government Agencies Privacy Code
items.quote: a PIA should be an integral part of the project planning process, not an afterthought
items.why: International comparator. Australia requires an impact assessment by law only of government agencies running high privacy risk projects, yet the regulator's test of a good one is the same as the UK's: early enough to change the design or stop the project, and evolving with it. Limits: Australian law and terminology (privacy impact assessment); guidance, not a binding rule for private organisations.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized.
items.why: The only free standard found that covers impact assessment for AI; the ISO impact-assessment standards are sold and their catalogue page blocked a plain request in the first pass. MAP 5.1 asks for the likelihood and size of each impact to be identified and documented, drawing on past incidents and outside feedback. Wider than a data protection assessment: it looks beyond personal data. Limits: voluntary United States framework, not UK law, and not a substitute for the Article 35 assessment.

items.title: Fairness and Data Protection Impact Assessments
items.publisher: Atoosa Kasirzadeh and Damian Clifford, AIES '21: Proceedings of the 2021 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (authors' copy on arXiv)
items.quote: they rarely mention the fairness principle in practice
items.why: Peer-reviewed analysis of regulators' guidance on impact assessments. Finds that although fairness should have a large place in the assessment, the guidance documents seldom mention it. Supports testing depth, not only existence: an assessment can follow the guidance and still miss whether the system treats people fairly. Limits: a review of guidance documents under the EU GDPR as they stood in 2021, not a study of assessments organisations have written; only the abstract is on the linked page.

items.title: An Institutional View of Algorithmic Impact Assessments
items.publisher: Andrew D. Selbst, Harvard Journal of Law & Technology vol. 35 no. 1
items.locator: Abstract, p. 117 of the volume (first page of the PDF)
items.quote: It is therefore inevitable that technology firms will have an amount of practical discretion in the assessment
items.why: Explains why impact assessments drift into paperwork: only the firm holds the knowledge needed, so it has wide discretion, and commercial incentives shape how it is used. Argues rules must be designed with that in mind. The best account found of the gap between the criterion's second and third levels. Limits: a United States law review article (student-edited), about proposed algorithmic impact assessments in the US, not the UK duty; argument drawing on organisational research, not new data.

items.title: Towards An Automated AI Act FRIA Tool That Can Reuse GDPR's DPIA
items.publisher: Tytti Rintamaki and Harshvardhan J. Pandit, arXiv (presented at the CLAIRvoyant workshop 2024)
items.quote: align the two to state where a DPIA can be reused in a FRIA
items.why: Bears on the top level of the criterion, reuse of the assessment as evidence. Maps the information in a data protection impact assessment against the EU AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment to show which parts carry over. Limits: a workshop paper on arXiv, not journal peer reviewed; EU law only; written before the 2026 changes to the AI Act, which amended the paragraph on reuse; only the abstract is on the linked page.
